Kitchen, meals & drinks · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

more adverb

a larger amount or number

also any more, give me more, I want more, more books, more food, more of, more than, more than (a number), more than enough, more time, much more, no more, nothing more, some more, would you like more, again (do it again), more! (again), more of this another time, more about this another time, anything else?, nothing else, nothing else, thanks

classical

Cic. Sen. 66: eō plūs viāticī quaerere
Traupman 347

plūs, plūris n. + gen.

neuter noun, used in the nominative and accusative, with the thing in the genitive · Declension on Wiktionary

more of a thing you measure: more food, more time, more milk

In the singular “more” is a noun, “a greater amount”, and what there is more of goes into the genitive: plūs cibī, more food; plūs temporis, more time; plūs lactis, more milk. On its own it is simply “more”: plūs volō, I want more. “Much more” is multō plūs; “more than enough”, plūs satis; “less” works the same way, minus labōris.

Other words

  • plūrēs, plūra — more of things you count: more balls, more books

    adjective, plural, agreeing with its noun; genitive plūrium · classical · Plin. Ep. 8.16.5: plūra fortasse quam dēbuī; sed pauciōra quam voluī; Traupman 347 · Declension on Wiktionary

    In the plural “more” is an adjective and agrees: plūrēs pilae, more balls; plūrēs librōs, more books; plūra, more things. So “give me more milk” is plūs lactis, but “give me more books” is plūrēs librōs. The singular with a genitive plural is classical too (plūs voluptātum, Cic. Fin. 1.62), but plūrēs is the everyday way. “Fewer” is pauciōrēs, never minus with a plural.

  • amplius — more, further, any more: something added to what there already is

    adverb, and a neuter used as a noun · classical · Hor. S. 2.6.4: nīl amplius ōrō; Traupman 347 · Wiktionary

    “More” in the sense of “further, in addition”: Vīs amplius?, would you like some more?; nihil amplius, nothing more. With a number, amplius and plūs mean “more than” and may drop quam without changing the case: amplius ducentōs, more than two hundred.

  • etiam — again, once more: more of doing something

    adverb, with an imperative · also used · classical · Plaut. Most. 2.2.43: Circumspice etiam (Lewis & Short) · Wiktionary

    (vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.)

    “More!” when what is wanted is the action again, not a larger amount: Lege etiam!, read some more; etiam atque etiam, again and again. With a plain statement etiam is “also, even”, so volō etiam is “I want it too”; “I want more” is plūs volō, and “even more”, etiam plūs.

Examples

  • Dā mihi plūs lactis.

    Give me more milk.composed

  • Plūrēs pilās volō.

    I want more balls.composed

  • Vīs amplius?

    Would you like some more?composed

  • potest enim quicquam esse absurdius quam, quō viae minus restet, eō plūs viāticī quaerere?

    can anything be sillier than to look for more provisions the less road is left?Cic. Sen. 66

  • neque enim tempus est ūllum, quō nōn plūs voluptātum habeat quam dolōrum

    for there is no time at which he does not have more pleasures than painsCic. Fin. 1.62

  • plūra fortasse quam dēbuī; sed pauciōra quam voluī

    more, perhaps, than I should have said; but less than I wanted toPlin. Ep. 8.16.5

  • an imitārī agrōs fertilēs, quī multō plūs efferunt quam accēpērunt?

    or to imitate fertile fields, which give back much more than they received?Cic. Off. 1.48

  • In eō proeliō nōn amplius ducentōs mīlitēs dēsīderāvit

    in that battle he lost no more than two hundred menCaes. BC 3.99.1

  • bene est. nīl amplius ōrō

    it is good. I ask for nothing moreHor. S. 2.6.4

  • sed plūra scrībēmus aliās

    but I’ll write more another timeCic. Fam. 7.6.2

  • successus improbōrum plūrēs allicit

    the success of the wicked lures more people onPhaedr. 2.3.7

  • Cui plūs licet quam pār est, plūs vult quam licet.

    Allow someone more than is fair, and he wants more than is allowed.Publil. Sent. C 22

  • Sed dē hōc aliās.

    But more of this another time.Cic. Lael. 1.1 (Lewis & Short s.v. redeō)

  • Sed dē hōc aliās plūribus.

    But more of this another time.Traupman 104

  • sed haec aliās plūribus

    but more of this another timeCic. Div. 2.2 (Lewis & Short s.v. alius)

  • Vīsne aliquid amplius?

    Do you want anything else?Traupman 68

  • Nihil amplius, grātiās.

    Nothing else, thanks.Traupman 68

  • Aliquid amplius?

    Anything else?Traupman 69

  • plūs pecūniae, vīrium, potentiae

    more money, strength, powerTraupman 347
